items.q: What's the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?

options.t: Vertical = a stronger machine; horizontal = more machines sharing the work
options.why: Right. Scale up (bigger box) or scale out (more boxes) — every architecture is some combination of these two moves. Vertical adds zero new problems; horizontal buys distributed-systems problems along with its capacity.

options.t: Vertical = scaling the database; horizontal = scaling the app servers
options.why: Both tiers can scale either way. A database can go vertical (bigger box, very common) or horizontal (sharding); app servers likewise. The axis is about how, not about which component.

options.t: Vertical = scaling reads; horizontal = scaling writes
options.why: Tempting because cloning (one horizontal move) does mainly scale reads — but that's the X-axis specifically. The vertical/horizontal split is about one machine vs many, not reads vs writes.

options.t: Vertical is on-premises; horizontal is cloud
options.why: Both exist everywhere. Clouds happily sell you a single 20TB-RAM monster (vertical) or 200 small VMs (horizontal); Stack Overflow scaled vertically on-prem for a decade.

items.q: Why must app servers be stateless before you can scale out behind a load balancer?

options.t: Because one user's consecutive requests can land on different servers
options.why: Exactly. Once requests bounce around the fleet, no server can privately hold data the next request needs. If server A keeps the session in its own memory, the user's next request to server B finds nothing — random logouts. State moves into signed tokens or a shared store so any server can handle any request.

options.t: Because holding state in process memory wastes RAM that the fleet could spend on request handling
options.why: Memory savings are incidental, and the state doesn't vanish anyway — it relocates to Redis or a cookie, and you pay for that RAM somewhere else. The point is interchangeability of servers, not thrift.

options.t: Because load balancers are only able to forward requests to servers that keep no state between requests
options.why: LBs happily forward anything — they can't even tell whether your app hoards state. That's exactly why the bug bites: the LB spreads requests obliviously, and the app breaks.

options.t: Because stateful servers can't be monitored properly
options.why: You can monitor stateful servers fine. The problem is correctness (lost sessions) and operability (can't kill or replace a server without losing its hoard), not observability.

items.q: What can a layer 4 load balancer see when deciding where to send traffic?

options.t: IP addresses and ports — nothing above the transport layer
options.why: Right. L4 reads the envelope, not the letter: source and destination IP and port, never the URL, headers, or cookies. It picks a backend when the TCP connection opens and forwards packets blind to their content — which is exactly why it's so fast and cheap per connection.

options.t: The full HTTP request line and headers, which it parses before choosing a backend
options.why: That's layer 7. An L4 balancer never parses HTTP at all — to read a request line it would have to terminate the connection and usually TLS, which is real work per request and exactly the price L7 pays for its routing brains.

options.t: Only the client's geographic location, resolved from the source IP before forwarding
options.why: Geo-awareness is a separate feature, usually DNS- or anycast-based, and IP-to-location lookup isn't something an L4 balancer does per packet. Its raw material is the packet's addressing fields, from which geography can only be crudely inferred.

options.t: The response time of each backend server
options.why: Backend latency is knowledge about servers, not about the packet — and it feeds the algorithm choice (like least-connections), which both L4 and L7 balancers can use. The L4/L7 split is about what's visible in the traffic itself.

items.q: When is plain round robin a perfectly good load-balancing algorithm?

options.t: When servers are identical and requests cost roughly the same
options.why: Yes. For a stateless API of short, similar requests on a uniform fleet, dealing requests in rotation is simple, even, and hard to beat. Fancier algorithms earn their keep only when those assumptions break.

options.t: Never — least connections is always strictly better
options.why: Least connections wins when request durations vary, but it costs tracking, and naive versions can herd traffic onto one briefly-idle server. When requests are uniform, round robin's simplicity is the senior choice.

options.t: When you need users to always hit the same server
options.why: That's the opposite of round robin — rotation guarantees users bounce between servers. Same-server affinity needs IP-hash or cookie stickiness.

options.t: Only for small fleets, where a big fleet's imbalances can't average out
options.why: Fleet size isn't the criterion, and the reasoning runs backwards — rotation is exactly as even across 300 servers as across 3. What matters is whether the requests themselves are uniform enough that even dealing means even load.

items.q: What's the difference between active and passive health checks?

options.t: Active = the LB probes a health endpoint on a schedule; passive = the LB watches real requests for errors
options.why: Right. Active checks poll (say GET /healthz every 5s, down after 3 failures); passive checks eject a server the moment real traffic starts failing. Production LBs run both: passive reacts fastest, active confirms recovery.

options.t: Active = checks that restart an unhealthy server automatically; passive = checks that only report the problem
options.why: Restarting is an orchestrator's job (like Kubernetes liveness), not the LB's. Both LB check types only decide whether the server stays in the routing rotation.

options.t: Active = checking the database; passive = checking the app process
options.why: That's the shallow-vs-deep axis — what the check inspects — and it's an important but different question. Active/passive is about how the LB learns: probing vs observing real traffic.

options.t: Active checks are for L7 balancers, passive for L4
options.why: Both kinds of balancer can do both kinds of check. An L4 balancer can probe a TCP port actively and watch connection failures passively.

items.q: What does connection draining do when you remove a server from the pool?

options.t: Stops sending it new requests but lets in-flight ones finish
options.why: Exactly. Drain = no new work, finish current work, with a deadline for stragglers (typically 30–300 seconds) after which the rest are cut. It's the mechanism that makes deploys and scale-downs invisible to users.

options.t: Slowly reduces the server's traffic share over several minutes
options.why: Close cousin, wrong direction — gradually ramping traffic is slow start, used when adding a cold server. Draining is a clean cut for new work: zero new requests, immediately.

options.t: Copies the server's open connections to another server
options.why: TCP connections can't be teleported between machines in a standard setup. That impossibility is exactly why draining exists: since you can't move in-flight work, you politely wait for it to finish.

options.t: Flushes the server's cache before shutdown
options.why: Draining is about requests, not caches. (Warming caches matters on the way in — that's why slow start exists — but drain concerns letting current requests complete gracefully.)

items.q: What is a sticky session?

options.t: Routing one user's requests always to the same backend server
options.why: Right — session affinity, usually via an LB-set cookie recording which backend served you. It lets stateful servers limp along behind an LB, at the cost of skewed load and painful deploys: statefulness in a load balancer costume.

options.t: A session that never expires
options.why: Session lifetime is an auth concern, unrelated to routing. Stickiness is about which server sees the requests, not how long the login lasts.

options.t: Storing the session in Redis so any server can serve any request
options.why: That's the opposite move — externalizing state is how you avoid ever needing stickiness in the first place. Sticky sessions leave state in one server's memory and bend the routing around it.

options.t: Caching the user's last response at the load balancer
options.why: Response caching is a real L7 feature but a different one. Stickiness pins the user to a server; it doesn't store any response content.

items.q: In an active-passive load balancer pair using VRRP, how does failover actually happen?

options.t: The standby stops hearing heartbeats and claims the shared virtual IP
options.why: Right. The VIP floats: the active LB heartbeats about every second, and after roughly three missed beats the standby broadcasts 'this IP now lives at my hardware address' (gratuitous ARP) and takes traffic within seconds. Clients keep using the same address — no DNS change, no client involvement.

options.t: The pair's DNS record is updated so that clients start resolving the name to the standby's own IP address
options.why: That's DNS failover — a different, slower layer (minutes, thanks to caching and TTL-ignoring resolvers). VRRP's entire appeal is that the IP itself moves, so nothing anywhere needs re-resolving.

options.t: Clients detect the failure and retry against a backup address
options.why: Client-side failover exists in some RPC systems, but VRRP requires zero client cooperation — clients keep dialing the same VIP and never learn anything happened.

options.t: The standby was already serving half the traffic and simply absorbs the rest
options.why: That's an active-active setup. In active-passive VRRP, the standby serves nothing until it claims the VIP — it's the theater understudy watching from the wings.

items.q: What is anycast, as used by CDN-style edge networks?

options.t: The same IP address is announced from many locations, and internet routing delivers each client to the nearest one
options.why: Right. BGP routing takes each packet to the topologically nearest site announcing that address. A failed site stops announcing and the internet re-routes around it in seconds — global failover with no DNS change at all.

options.t: DNS inspects where each query comes from and returns a different IP address for each client's region
options.why: That's GeoDNS — a real technique, but it lives in DNS and inherits DNS's caching delays. Anycast works below DNS: one address, many places, routing does the steering.

options.t: The client sends each request to every server and uses the fastest reply
options.why: Sending to all and racing replies would multiply traffic enormously. With anycast the client sends one packet to one address; the network picks which site receives it.

options.t: A protocol for broadcasting content to many users at once
options.why: That's closer to multicast. Anycast is one-to-nearest-one: many sites share an address, each client reaches exactly one of them.

items.q: You add a second app server behind a load balancer. Immediately, users report being randomly logged out every few clicks. Most likely cause?

options.t: Sessions live in each server's memory, not in a shared store
options.why: The classic day-one symptom of scaling a stateful app: the LB spreads one user's clicks across both servers, and requests landing on server B can't find sessions created on server A. Fix: signed tokens the client carries, or a shared session store — make the servers stateless.

options.t: The load balancer is dropping cookies from requests
options.why: Standard LBs pass cookies through untouched — silently eating headers would break half the internet. The cookie arrives fine; it's the server-side lookup behind it that fails on the 'wrong' machine.

options.t: The second server's clock is out of sync, expiring tokens early
options.why: Clock skew can cause token weirdness, but it wouldn't produce the every-few-clicks alternating pattern — and 'logged out roughly half the time, randomly' right after adding a server points straight at per-server memory.

options.t: The session table in the database is overloaded by the extra server
options.why: If sessions were in a shared database, both servers would see them — that architecture doesn't produce this bug. The symptom exists precisely because sessions are NOT shared.

items.q: Your service mixes 50ms API calls with file uploads that take 30–120 seconds. Under round robin, some servers periodically melt while others idle. Best fix at the LB?

options.t: Least connections — busy servers stop receiving new work
options.why: This is the textbook least-connections workload: high variance in request duration. Open-connection count is a live proxy for busyness, so servers stuck with slow uploads naturally stop being dealt new requests and the algorithm self-corrects the pileups round robin creates. (Even better long-term: split uploads onto their own pool via L7 path routing.)

options.t: Weighted round robin with higher weights on the bigger servers
options.why: Weights fix heterogeneous servers, not heterogeneous requests. The melt happens because rotation ignores what each server is currently stuck with — static weights can't see that either.

options.t: IP hash, so upload-heavy users stay on their own servers
options.why: This concentrates the problem instead of spreading it: an upload-heavy user now hammers one specific server forever, and a NAT full of users behind one IP makes it worse.

options.t: Add more servers until round robin's unevenness stops mattering
options.why: Capacity can mask an algorithm mismatch, but you're paying for idle servers to absorb bad routing. Matching the algorithm to the workload's variance is free.

items.q: You need to route /video/* requests to a GPU transcoding pool and everything else to the general fleet — and terminate TLS in one place. What must sit at that decision point?

options.t: A layer 7 load balancer, terminating TLS and routing on the path
options.why: Path-based routing requires reading the HTTP request, and reading the request requires terminating the connection and TLS — so both of your requirements land on the same box. That's the definition of an L7 balancer's job: NGINX, Envoy, HAProxy, ALB.

options.t: A layer 4 load balancer — it's faster, and speed matters for video
options.why: An L4 balancer never sees the URL — the path is inside encrypted content it can't open. It's physically unable to make this routing decision, no matter how fast it forwards packets.

options.t: DNS — give video.example.com its own IP pointing at the GPU pool
options.why: Workable only if you can change every client to use the new hostname, and it splits your TLS story across entry points. The question as posed — route by path, one TLS termination — is squarely L7.

options.t: The app servers — have them redirect video requests to the GPU pool
options.why: This costs an extra round trip per video request and burns general-fleet capacity as a redirect layer. Content routing is exactly the work an L7 balancer exists to do at the front door.

items.q: During a 15-second database blip, your load balancer marked all 12 app servers unhealthy and served errors for a full minute — even though cached reads would have worked. What was the design mistake?

options.t: The health check pinged the database, so every server failed it at once
options.why: Right — that's a deep check in the traffic-removal path. Deep checks fail simultaneously fleet-wide when a shared dependency hiccups, converting a partial degradation into a self-inflicted total outage. LB checks should be shallow (process up, can serve), with dependency failures handled per-request, plus fail-open when 'everyone' looks down.

options.t: The probe interval was too long — faster probes would have fixed this
options.why: Faster probes would have taken the fleet down faster. The timing isn't the flaw; checking a shared dependency in the fleet-removal path is.

options.t: There were too few servers — more would have kept some healthy
options.why: Every server's deep check pings the same database, so 12 or 200, they all fail together. Correlated failure doesn't dilute with fleet size — that's exactly what makes deep checks dangerous.

options.t: The health endpoint should have been cached for 60 seconds
options.why: Caching health responses just delays truth in both directions — slow to detect real death, slow to confirm recovery. The fix is checking the right thing, not checking a stale copy of the wrong thing.

items.q: Every deploy, a burst of users see failed requests at the moment each server restarts. Which sequence eliminates this?

options.t: Drain the server first, deploy, then readmit it with slow start
options.why: The full zero-downtime recipe: make the server deliberately fail its own health check, wait for the LB to stop sending traffic and for in-flight requests to finish (with a deadline for stragglers), then deploy, then let the checks readmit it while slow start ramps it back up warm. Each mechanism is standard LB configuration — the skill is the sequence.

options.t: Deploy at 3am when traffic is lowest, so only a handful of users hit the window
options.why: Fewer victims is not zero victims — and it institutionalizes 3am work and a slow release cadence, which quietly costs far more than the errors did. The mechanical fix costs nothing and works at noon.

options.t: Speed up the restart so the error window is under a second
options.why: A shorter window still kills every request in flight during it, and at thousands of req/s that's real users every deploy. Draining makes the window's length irrelevant.

options.t: Have clients retry failed requests automatically with backoff
options.why: Retries with backoff are a good safety net, but as the primary mechanism they mask the wound: non-idempotent requests can't be blindly retried (chapter 2.2), and you're shipping errors on purpose. Fix the cause at the LB.

items.q: After enabling IP-hash affinity, one server runs at 90% CPU while the rest idle. Traffic logs show a huge share of requests from a single IP address. What's happening?

options.t: Thousands of users share that one IP behind a NAT gateway
options.why: The classic IP-hash failure. A carrier or campus NAT makes one IP represent an entire region or office, and hashing on it lumps that whole crowd onto one backend. Fix: cookie-based stickiness (which distinguishes users behind shared IPs) or drop affinity and externalize the state.

options.t: A DDoS attack from that IP
options.why: Worth ruling out, but a NAT'd user population shows normal, well-formed, logged-in traffic patterns — organic requests from many accounts. An attack profile looks different, and the load appearing exactly when you enabled IP-hash is the giveaway.

options.t: The hash function is biased toward that server
options.why: A biased hash would skew traffic from many IPs, not concentrate one enormous IP. The hash is doing its job — same input, same server — the input is just carrying a hidden crowd.

options.t: That server advertises a higher weight to the balancer
options.why: Weights would draw proportionally more traffic from all sources, not a flood from one address. The single-IP signature points at NAT lumping, not configuration.

items.q: Your two data centers fail over via DNS with a 60-second TTL. In a real failover, some users stayed broken for 20+ minutes. Why?

options.t: Resolvers and apps cached the old answer well past the TTL
options.why: The dirty secret of DNS failover: you set the TTL, but many resolvers ignore it entirely. ISP resolvers, OS caches, and long-lived app processes (like JVMs with default settings) may hold stale answers for minutes to hours. DNS failover is disaster recovery measured in minutes, never high availability measured in seconds.

options.t: 60 seconds is too long a TTL — 5 seconds would fix it
options.why: A shorter TTL trims the honest resolvers' delay (at the cost of far more DNS query load) but does nothing about the dishonest ones — the TTL-ignoring caches are exactly who kept those users broken for 20 minutes.

options.t: DNS can only point at one IP address at a time
options.why: DNS happily returns multiple records and health-checked answers (that's how Route 53 failover works). The problem isn't expressiveness — it's that cached answers live on beyond your control.

options.t: The users' browsers didn't support DNS failover
options.why: There's no browser feature to support — failover happens in the resolution chain. The stale-cache problem lives in resolvers and OS caches, which is precisely why it's outside anyone's quick control.

items.q: Autoscaling adds three servers during a spike. Each new server immediately tanks: 5-second latencies for its first minute, then fine. What's the missing mechanism?

options.t: Slow start — ramp a new server's traffic up as it warms
options.why: A cold server (empty local cache, unwarmed runtime, empty connection pools) can't take a full share in its first seconds. Slow start at the LB moves it from a trickle to a full share over a window; pre-warming critical caches before it passes the health check helps too. It's the mirror image of draining.

options.t: Bigger instances, so cold servers have the headroom to absorb the first minute
options.why: A bigger cold server is still cold — the first requests miss every cache and open every connection fresh regardless of core count, and headroom doesn't populate a cache. You'd pay permanently for a problem that lasts sixty seconds.

options.t: Sticky sessions, so new servers only take new users and warm up gradually
options.why: Stickiness does accidentally shelter a new server — only new users land there — but it inflicts skewed load and hostile deploys permanently to soften one minute of warm-up. Slow start does the same sheltering surgically, then stops.

options.t: Scale up earlier so servers are warm before the spike
options.why: Predictive scaling is a genuinely useful complement for known patterns (the 9pm surge), but spikes you can't predict still arrive — the fleet must be able to admit a cold server gracefully at any time.

items.q: A legacy app keeps shopping carts in server memory and can't be rewritten this quarter. It must scale to four servers now. Most defensible immediate setup?

options.t: Cookie-based sticky sessions at the L7 balancer, named as temporary debt
options.why: Stickiness is exactly the pragmatic bridge for un-rewritable stateful apps — that's its legitimate use case. The senior part is naming the costs you're accepting (skewed load, deploys log users out of one server's carts, a crash wipes carts) and putting cart externalization on the roadmap with a date.

options.t: IP-hash affinity at the L4 balancer — same effect, and no cookies needed
options.why: IP-hash gives crude affinity but breaks for the NAT crowd, and for mobile users whose IP changes mid-session it silently loses the cart. Cookie stickiness identifies the actual user; if you must be sticky, be sticky precisely.

options.t: Round robin, accepting occasional cart loss until the rewrite
options.why: Round robin makes carts vanish on nearly every click, not occasionally — each request lands on a random server holding a different (mostly empty) cart. That's shipping a broken product, not accepting a trade-off.

options.t: Refuse to scale until carts move to Redis — fix the root cause first
options.why: Directionally right about the end state, but 'no capacity until the rewrite lands' fails the business now, and the rewrite is explicitly off the table this quarter. Senior judgment ships the bridge (stickiness), names its debt, and schedules the payoff.

items.q: Interview: 'Design the backend for a B2B analytics dashboard — 5,000 companies, about 1,200 requests/second at peak.' A candidate opens with a 15-microservice Kubernetes architecture across three regions. What does the senior version of this answer look like?

options.t: "1,200 req/s fits on a few stateless app servers behind an L7 balancer in a VRRP pair, plus one Postgres and a replica — and here's the growth signal that would change that."
options.why: The numbers say this is a small system — Stack Overflow served a top-100 site with nine underworked web servers. Committing to the simple design, making the LB redundant (the actual SPOF), and naming the escalation trigger reads as judgment. Complexity without numbers behind it reads as insecurity.

options.t: The microservices answer is right — B2B customers demand enterprise-grade architecture, and building it early avoids a painful migration when the client list grows
options.why: 'Enterprise-grade' is a label, not a load number. Fifteen services means fifteen deploy pipelines and network hops in exchange for solving no problem this workload has — interviewers read unjustified complexity as inexperience with its costs.

options.t: Split the difference: five microservices and one region
options.why: Negotiating complexity downward without a reason is still architecture by vibes. The senior move derives the design from the numbers, and 1,200 req/s doesn't demand service decomposition at all.

options.t: Ask the interviewer whether they would rather see a microservices design or a simple one before committing either way
options.why: The numbers already answered the design question — outsourcing it back is the waiting-to-be-led pattern. If you want to hedge, do it by naming the trigger that would change your answer, which shows range without abandoning the commitment.

items.q: Your stateless web tier autoscales beautifully. Traffic grows 10x over six months. What most likely breaks first, and what does the senior answer sound like?

options.t: The shared stateful tiers — the database and session store — because cloning app servers funnels more load into them
options.why: The X-axis scales compute and reads, never writes or data size. Every clone opens more connections and sends more queries to the same stateful backends — the bottleneck doesn't disappear, it migrates downstream. The senior answer names that and reaches for caching (1.6), replicas (1.8), then sharding (1.9), in that order.

options.t: Nothing — stateless app servers plus autoscaling is precisely the design that absorbs 10x traffic; handling growth without redesign is the whole point of building it this way
options.why: 'It autoscales' is a claim about one tier. The interviewer's 10x push exists precisely to see whether you know cloning app servers just aims a bigger firehose at the shared state behind them.

options.t: The load balancer — 10x traffic will overwhelm it
options.why: A plausible-sounding guess, but LBs are the sturdiest tier here: L7 boxes handle tens of thousands of req/s each and scale out behind L4/anycast fronts. At 10x, the database is screaming long before the LB sweats.

options.t: The autoscaler itself — it can't add servers fast enough
options.why: Scaling lag is a real operational wrinkle (mitigated by headroom and predictive scaling), but it's a speed bump, not the structural wall. The wall is that no number of clones scales the write path.

items.q: Interviewer: 'You've drawn one load balancer. It's a single point of failure — fix it.' Which answer earns the senior grade?

options.t: "Inside the site: an active-passive VRRP pair sharing a VIP, seconds to fail over. Across sites: anycast, or DNS failover with its honest minutes-long tail."
options.why: Layers plus time scales plus an honest limitation — that's the complete answer. It shows you know the VIP mechanism, that clients keep the same address, what it protects (a box, not a building), and that DNS failover drags because resolvers ignore TTLs. Precision about failover time is what separates recall from operation.

options.t: "Add a second load balancer, publish both addresses in DNS round robin, and let clients spread themselves across the pair."
options.why: Half a mechanism: DNS round robin spreads load but doesn't detect death — clients keep receiving the dead LB's IP until caches expire, so roughly half of requests fail for minutes. Without health-checked DNS or a floating VIP, this doesn't remove the SPOF, it duplicates it.

options.t: "Use a managed cloud load balancer — AWS runs it replicated across zones, so redundancy becomes the provider's problem instead of mine."
options.why: Correct as a practical deployment choice, and worth saying — but stopping there dodges the question being asked, which is whether you understand the mechanism. Say 'managed LBs are redundant internally — here's how that works: VIP failover within a zone, anycast across zones.'

options.t: "Load balancers basically never fail — they're simple, battle-tested boxes, so the SPOF is theoretical."
options.why: Everything fails: hardware dies, configs get fat-fingered, kernels panic. Waving off a named SPOF is the single fastest way to fail a senior round — the entire question exists to check whether you take failure seriously.

items.q: A teammate proposes sticky sessions so each user's requests hit a server with their data already in local cache — 'it cut p50 latency 40% in testing.' What's the senior evaluation?

options.t: Accept affinity only as an optimization — landing on the 'wrong' server must still work
options.why: The line that matters: affinity for performance (miss = slower) is defensible; affinity for correctness (miss = broken) is statefulness sneaking back in. Insist on the graceful-degradation path through the shared cache tier, and weigh the 40% against skewed load and harder deploys before shipping.

options.t: Reject it — sticky sessions are a known anti-pattern, so a latency number can't justify one
options.why: Rules-lawyering the heuristic misses its reason. The prohibition targets correctness-critical stickiness; cache-locality affinity with a working fallback is a legitimate optimization pattern (it's how affinity-aware routing works in serious systems). Absolute rules read junior; reasons read senior.

options.t: Accept it — a measured 40% p50 win outweighs theoretical objections
options.why: A p50 benchmark from testing doesn't capture the operational bill: load skew under real traffic mixes, deploys that dump sessions, autoscaling that only feeds new servers. Benchmarks are evidence, not verdicts — the senior weighs the whole ledger.

options.t: Counter-propose replicating every user's cache entries to every server, so any server is fast
options.why: Full replication trades the problem for a worse one: N copies of everything caps your cache's effective size at one server's RAM and multiplies invalidation traffic on every write. The shared cache tier (chapter 1.6) exists precisely to avoid both extremes.

items.q: Design review: a proposed /healthz for app servers checks the process, the database, Redis, and two internal services, and the LB removes any server failing it. The author says 'we should never route to a server that can't fully serve.' Your call?

options.t: Veto the deep check in the LB path — shallow check for routing, deep signals for monitoring
options.why: The author's principle sounds rigorous but has a fleet-wide failure mode: any shared dependency blip fails every server's check at once and the LB removes everything — a self-inflicted total outage where cached reads could have survived. Handle dependencies per-request with fallbacks, fail open above an unhealthy-fraction threshold, and keep the deep signals in monitoring and rollout readiness instead.

options.t: Approve — never routing to a server that can't fully serve is exactly the rigor that protects users from degraded, half-working responses
options.why: The hidden assumption is that failures are independent per-server. Dependency failures are correlated across the whole fleet, so this policy's real behavior is 'when the database blinks, serve nothing to anyone.' Degraded service beats no service.

options.t: Approve, but lengthen the probe interval so blips get absorbed
options.why: Tuning timing on a structurally wrong check trades one failure for another: long intervals absorb blips but leave genuinely dead servers receiving traffic for ages. The problem is what the check measures, not how often.

options.t: Compromise: deep-check half the fleet, shallow-check the other half
options.why: Now a database blip removes exactly half your capacity at the worst moment, and you've doubled the configs to reason about during an incident. Split-brain policies are complexity with no principle behind them.

items.q: Your CTO wants to 'do microservices this year' for a monolith serving 800 req/s with a healthy database, citing scale. Applying the scale cube honestly, what's the senior counsel?

options.t: "We have X-axis headroom for years at 800 req/s; the honest case for Y-splitting is team autonomy, not scale."
options.why: The scale cube's real teaching: X (clones behind the LB) handles raw traffic cheaply; Y's primary payoff is teams not blocking each other on deploys; Z is for when data outgrows a box. Naming which axis solves which problem — and refusing to buy operational complexity for a problem you don't have — is exactly the judgment the cube encodes. Pinterest's retro is the canonical evidence.

options.t: Support it — microservices are how serious companies scale, and preparing early avoids a painful migration later
options.why: Pinterest scaled to tens of millions of users on cloned web servers and sharded MySQL with a handful of engineers. 'Preparing early' for scale you may never see means paying the distributed-systems tax (network failures, tracing, deploy orchestration) every day starting now.

options.t: Refuse — monoliths should never be split; microservices are a fad the industry is already walking back
options.why: The mirror-image dogma. Y-axis splits are the right call when deploy contention or team coupling is the real bottleneck — the failure is splitting for a reason you don't have, not splitting ever.

options.t: Propose sharding the database instead — it delivers real scalability without touching the application's architecture
options.why: That's the Z-axis, which solves data-size and write-throughput problems — and 'a healthy database' means you don't have one. Swapping an unneeded Y move for an unneeded Z move is trading complexity for complexity.

items.q: Black Friday postmortem: at 10x normal traffic, autoscaling worked, but every scale-out event caused a 30-second latency spike, and one LB config push at peak dropped 2% of requests for a minute. Which remediation list reads senior?

options.t: "Slow start plus cache pre-warming for the cold-server spikes; treat LB config pushes as deploys and canary them; alert on per-server p99."
options.why: Each item maps a symptom to its mechanism: cold servers ramp instead of taking a full share, and warm their caches before passing health checks; the config drop gets change management for the LB itself (the most under-respected deploy surface in production); and queue-depth plus per-server p99 alerts catch the next one early. Specific, mechanical, operational — the senior signature.

options.t: "Increase the minimum fleet size and keep standing headroom so autoscaling rarely needs to trigger during peak season at all."
options.why: Paying for idle servers year-round to avoid fixing a 30-second warm-up is treating the bill as the cure. It also leaves the real finding — you can't admit a cold server gracefully — unfixed for the day the fleet must grow anyway.

options.t: "Move everything to a bigger managed LB tier and trust the provider to handle peak season."
options.why: The incidents were about your fleet's warm-up behavior and your config process — neither moves to the provider with the hardware. Vendor-shifting without a mechanism naming what changes is the buzzword reflex.

options.t: "Freeze all changes during peak season so nothing can break while traffic is high."
options.why: Change freezes have their place, but as the whole answer they concede you can't operate safely — and the cold-server spikes weren't even change-induced; they were organic scaling. Fix the mechanics; then freezes become a choice, not a crutch.
